segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Come now, you rich people, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Your wealth has rotted, and your clothes have become moth-eaten.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, the wages of the workers who mowed your fields, the wages you kept back, are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You have condemned, you have murdered the righteous one. Does he not oppose you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be patient, therefore, brothers and sisters, until the coming of the Lord. Look, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it until it receives the early and the late rain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You too must be patient. Strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord has drawn near.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not grumble against one another, brothers and sisters, so that you may not be judged. Look, the judge is standing at the doors.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, take as an example of suffering hardship and of patience the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the outcome the Lord brought about, that the Lord is deeply compassionate and merciful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Above all, my brothers and sisters, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or with any other oath. Let your yes be yes and your no be no, so that you do not fall under judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is anyone among you suffering hardship? Let them pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let them sing praise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is anyone among you sick? Let them call for the elders of the assembly, and let the elders pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and if they have committed sins, they will be forgiven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. The petition of a righteous person has great power as it takes effect.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Elijah was a human being with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three years and six months.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: My brothers and sisters, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone turns them back,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: let that person know that whoever turns a sinner back from their wandering way will save their soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

notes.traditional: will eat your flesh like fire
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and 'like fire' can go with either sentence. Most translations attach it to what precedes, as here. The Greek edition translated here places the break earlier, which would give 'It is fire, as it were, that you have stored up in the last days.' Either division is possible.

notes.traditional: Lord of Sabaoth; Lord of hosts; Lord Almighty
notes.note: James keeps the Hebrew word Sabaoth, 'armies', as the Greek version of Isaiah often does. The title presents God as commander of the heavenly armies, and it is used here for the one who hears the cries of defrauded workers. 'Hosts' is the long-established English form of the title.

notes.traditional: the just; the righteous person; the innocent one
notes.note: One Greek word covers what English divides into 'righteous', 'just' and 'innocent'. Most interpreters take it generically here, of the innocent poor whom the rich ruin through the courts. A minority see a reference to Jesus, who is called 'the Righteous One' elsewhere in the New Testament.

Most translations read this as a statement, 'he does not resist you', picturing a victim who cannot fight back. The Greek edition translated here punctuates it as a question. On that reading the one who now opposes the rich is either the righteous victim or God, of whom the same verb is used in 4:6. Both readings are grammatical, and the choice rests on punctuation that the earliest manuscripts did not have.

The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and James is writing to whole communities. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers', while many recent ones have 'brothers and sisters'. The longer phrase is used here because 'brothers' alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed.

notes.phrase: the early and the late rain
notes.traditional: the early and the late rains
notes.note: The Greek has only 'early and late'; 'rain' is understood, and some manuscripts add it. In the eastern Mediterranean the autumn rains soften the ground for sowing and the spring rains swell the grain before harvest. A farmer depends on both, and the pairing is a stock phrase from Israel's Scriptures.

'The patience of Job' is proverbial in English, but the Greek word here is not the one translated 'patience' in verses 7–10. It means holding out under pressure, which suits a Job who protests loudly yet does not give up on God. Most modern translations likewise use 'endurance', 'perseverance' or 'steadfastness'.

notes.phrase: the outcome the Lord brought about
notes.traditional: the end of the Lord; the purpose of the Lord
notes.note: Literally 'the end of the Lord'. The word can mean an outcome or a goal, so the phrase is either what the Lord finally did for Job, the restoration at the close of the book, or the Lord's purpose in the whole affair. Most interpreters prefer the first sense, which is followed here.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, and in the Greek Scriptures Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and its reference is clear, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word.

notes.traditional: will save the sick; will make the sick person well
notes.note: The Greek verb means to rescue, and is used both of healing from illness and of final salvation. Here physical recovery is in view first, and many translations render it 'make well' or 'restore'. 'Save' is kept because the next clauses speak of forgiveness and because the same verb returns in verse 20. 'Raise up' can likewise mean getting up from a sickbed or resurrection.

notes.traditional: the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much
notes.note: The Greek participle can be read as 'when it is at work', that is, in its effect, or as 'when it is made effective', that is, by God. Older translations took it as describing the prayer's intensity ('fervent'). The meaning is disputed, and the rendering here follows the first reading.

The story is in 1 Kings 17–18, which says that rain returned 'in the third year' and does not record Elijah praying for the drought. The figure of three and a half years also appears in Luke 4:25 and seems to reflect a Jewish tradition of retelling the story.

notes.traditional: shall save a soul from death; will save his soul from death
notes.note: The Greek 'his soul' does not say whose, and the English 'their' leaves it equally open. Most interpreters take it as the sinner's soul, rescued from death, but the sins covered could be the sinner's or the rescuer's. The word translated 'soul' means the person's life or self, not a separable part of them. Manuscripts also vary slightly in the wording of this phrase.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed communities recurs in every letter and Acts, and translations split between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters', so one policy is needed.
The verb covers both healing and salvation across the Gospels, Acts and the letters, and the choice between 'save', 'heal' and 'make well' needs a consistent rule.
Translators alternate between 'soul', 'life' and 'self' throughout the New Testament, and 'soul' can import later ideas of an immaterial part of a person.
It is rendered variously 'patience', 'perseverance', 'steadfastness' and 'endurance' across books, and it must be kept distinct from μακροθυμία ('patience').
A transliterated Hebrew title occurring only here and in Romans 9:29, where the choice among 'Sabaoth', 'of Hosts', 'of Armies' and 'Almighty' should be made once.
